_about: End-to-end scenarios for scripts/scenarios.js. Each one starts a real run through the app's own API, plays the person from a script (answers, pick), then checks two things: the FLOW (did the app do what the settings say?) and the OUTCOME (did the builds work? hidden tests the agents never see, from checks/). Kept small on purpose: one or two ideas each, one carried forward. Scenarios marked "set": "hard" run only with --set hard: each harder task runs twice, once with help allowed and once alone, so the hidden tests show what asking changed.

scenarios.title: Lean: press Start on a bug hunt, nobody at the screen

run.problem: Read README.md: support reports that some customers paid nothing for their order, and some say their discount code did nothing. Find the cause or causes, using the code, the data, CHANGELOG.md and logs/orders.log, then fix them with a test for each. Say what in the log is not related.

scenarios.title: Facilitator: agents may ask before they start and stop for help; one decision only the person knows

run.problem: Add tags to notes in this command-line notebook (read README.md): a person can tag a note when adding it and list only the notes with a tag. Constraints: existing notes files (version 1) must still load and other scripts must still read the files; no new dependencies; the existing tests keep passing; add tests for the new behaviour. The person who set this task has already decided the exact command-line syntax for tags, and it is not written anywhere: ask them.

person._answers: The first answer whose match (a regular expression, case ignored) fits the question is given; an empty match fits any question.

answers.answer: Add with: add "text" --tag NAME (the flag can be repeated). List with: list --tag NAME, which shows only the notes with that tag. Tag names are lowercase words.
Keep "version": 1. The other scripts ignore fields they do not know, so an optional tags field is fine.
Use your own judgement and keep it small.

scenarios.title: The person chooses blind what gets built, from a brief an agent wrote from one line

run.problem: Some customers paid nothing for their order. Find out why and fix it.
run.criteria:
Explains the evidence in the log
Fix is small and correct

scenarios.title: Harder: time zones and clock changes; agents may stop and ask the person for the unwritten rules

run.problem: Read README.md: users report reminders arriving at the wrong time around the clock changes, and on the wrong day for some monthly reminders. Make every reminder fire at the right local time and on the right day all year, in any time zone, with tests for what you fix. Keep nextRun and runs as they are called today; no new dependencies. A few edge cases follow rules the team has decided but not written down: if you meet one, ask rather than guess.

answers.answer: Here are the team's rules. When a month does not have the day asked for (the 31st in April, the 30th in February), the reminder fires on the last day of that month, and goes back to the day asked for the month after. When the time does not exist that night because the clocks jump forward, move it forward by the hour the clocks skip: 01:30 becomes 02:30. When the time happens twice because the clocks go back, it fires only the first time.

scenarios.title: Harder: a real CSV export with quotes, line breaks, Excel marks and duplicates; agents may stop and ask

run.problem: Read README.md: the sales team reports broken imports from their CRM export (data/export.csv is a real one). Make importContacts read every export correctly, with tests for what you fix. Keep importContacts as it is called today; no new dependencies. A few cases follow rules the team has decided but not written down: if you meet one, ask rather than guess.

answers.answer: Here are the team's rules. The same email, in any mix of upper and lower case, is the same person: keep one contact with the values of the most recently updated row, and fill any of its empty fields from the older rows. Rows without a usable email are skipped and counted in skipped. Keep names as they are written.

scenarios.title: Technical: a calculator that must follow an exact spec (precedence, brackets, error positions)
scenarios.learn: Do agents write a real grammar or patch the old loop, and does anyone meet the exact error format? 12 graded cases should separate careful from quick.

run.problem: Read README.md: the calculator only works left to right. Make evaluate follow the spec in README.md exactly, including the error messages, with tests. No new dependencies.

scenarios.title: Technical: make a slow function fast without changing a single output
scenarios.learn: Do agents measure before and after, and keep the output identical (order of ties, apostrophes) while making it fast?

run.problem: Read README.md: topWords never finishes on a whole book. Make it fast on large texts without changing its output in any case, and show how much faster it is. No new dependencies.

scenarios.title: Build: a chart for a printed report, black and white
scenarios.learn: Do agents read the data before drawing (the August dip), respect the black-and-white constraint, and how different do their charts look? Pictures in the report.

run.problem: Read README.md and make the chart it asks for, as chart.svg in the current folder. Write it by hand or with a small script in plain Node.js (no libraries).
run.criteria:
Readable when printed in black and white
Shows what matters in the data
Clean and honest (no distorted scales)

scenarios.title: Build, open-ended: an animation that explains the blind vote to a 12-year-old
scenarios.learn: On an open visual brief, how different are the ideas, does the vote reward ambition, and does what they build actually run and move? Frames in the report.

run.problem: In the current (empty) folder, make index.html: a self-contained looping animation (no network, no libraries) that explains to a 12-year-old, in about 20 seconds, how a blind vote between AI agents works: several agents propose ideas, the ideas are shown without names, nobody scores their own, and the best average wins.

scenarios.title: Think and document: a decision record grounded in the code
scenarios.learn: When the deliverable is writing, do agents ground claims in the real code (every file and function they name exists), keep the word limit, and reach the same recommendation?

run.problem: The team behind this shop argues about money: keep amounts as integer cents in plain numbers, or introduce a Money type. Read the code, the data and CHANGELOG.md, then write DECISION.md in the current folder: the options, their trade-offs for this code, a recommendation, and what would change our mind. At most 500 words, with sections Options, Recommendation and What would change our mind. Refer to the code by file paths and function names in backticks. Do not change the code.
run.criteria:
Grounded in this code, not generic
Clear recommendation
Honest about the costs

scenarios.title: Open-ended document: a guide for a new contributor to this app, with questions first
scenarios.learn: On a real codebase they have not seen, how much of what agents write about the code is true (files and functions that exist), and do they ask questions on an open brief?

run.problem: Write GUIDE.md for a new contributor to this app (its code is in the current folder): how one run flows from the Start button to the patches, which file does what, and where to make a first change safely. At most 900 words. Name real files and functions in backticks so readers can find them. Do not change the code.

answers.answer: Write for someone who knows JavaScript but has never seen this app. Practical over complete.
